questions.scenario: A bank's Jenkins controller is slow and occasionally crashes during busy periods. Builds run directly on the controller.
questions.question: What is the recommended architecture change?
options: Run all builds sequentially
Run builds on separate agents (VMs, containers or Kubernetes pods) and keep the controller for scheduling and configuration
Give the controller more plugins
Move the Jenkinsfile into the Jenkins UI
questions.explanation: Builds on the controller compete with scheduling and can affect its security and stability. Agents isolate and scale build workloads.

questions.scenario: A Jenkinsfile contains sh "docker login -u ${REG_USER} -p ${REG_PASS} registry.example.ng" inside withCredentials.
questions.question: What is the risk and fix?
options: Credentials must be hard-coded in the Jenkinsfile instead
There is no risk because Jenkins masks everything
Groovy interpolates the secret into the command string, where it can leak via logs or process lists; use single quotes so the shell expands it, and pass the password with --password-stdin
docker login cannot be used in Jenkins
questions.explanation: Double-quoted Groovy strings interpolate secrets before the shell runs. Letting the shell read environment variables, and avoiding passwords on the command line, keeps them out of logs.

questions.scenario: Production deployments from a Jenkins pipeline must be approved by a member of the release-managers group.
questions.question: Which declarative feature implements this?
options: A buildDiscarder option
A parallel block
An input directive on the deployment stage with submitter 'release-managers'
A post { success { ... } } block
questions.explanation: The input directive pauses the pipeline until an authorised user approves, which is recorded in the build history.

questions.scenario: An Azure DevOps pipeline stores the Azure Container Registry admin password in a pipeline variable to push images.
questions.question: What is the better practice?
options: Mark the variable as not secret so it is easier to debug
Disable authentication on the registry
Put the password in azure-pipelines.yml
Use a service connection (ideally with workload identity federation) so the pipeline authenticates without a stored password
questions.explanation: Service connections centralise and restrict credentials; workload identity federation removes long-lived secrets, like OIDC in GitHub Actions.

questions.scenario: You are mapping a GitHub Actions workflow to Azure Pipelines.
questions.question: Which mappings are correct? (Choose two.)
options: GitHub environment with required reviewers → Azure Pipelines environment with approvals and checks
GitHub action (uses:) → Azure Pipelines task (for example Docker@2)
GitHub runner → Azure Boards work item
GitHub secrets → Azure Repos branch policy
questions.explanation: Environments with approvals and reusable building blocks map directly. Runners map to agents/pools, and secrets to secret variables or Key Vault.

questions.scenario: A platform team supports 150 services on Jenkins and wants every service to use the same build, test, scan and publish steps.
questions.question: Which Jenkins feature is designed for this?
options: Copying the full pipeline into each job's configuration page
A shared library exposing a standard pipeline step that each Jenkinsfile calls
Disabling Jenkinsfiles
One giant job that builds all services
questions.explanation: Shared libraries version and centralise pipeline logic, like reusable workflows in GitHub or templates in Azure Pipelines.

questions.scenario: A bank is moving from Jenkins to GitHub Actions and wants to avoid a risky big-bang switch.
questions.question: What is a sensible migration approach?
options: Let each team design its own pipeline without gates
Switch every service in one weekend and delete Jenkins
Migrate service by service, keeping the same stages and gates, and retire each Jenkins job only after the new pipeline has deployed to production
Remove quality gates during migration to save time
questions.explanation: Incremental migration with equivalent controls keeps change-management evidence continuous and limits blast radius.
